These evidence-based  recommendations were created with the consensus of the subcommittee members, taking into  consideration unique characteristics of bacteriology and antimicrobial susceptibilities of AOM  pathogens in Japan, as well as global advances in vaccines.

Methods: The subcommittee re-evaluated key clinical issues based on SCOPE (a master plan  of the guidelines) and created clinical questions (CQ) about the diagnosis and management of  AOM patients. A literature search of the publications from 2013 to 2016 were added to the  Guidelines 2013, not only to assess the evidence on the effectiveness of vaccines, but also to  provide up to date information of the bacteriology and antimicrobial susceptibilities of AOM  causative pathogens in Japan.

1. Introduction

The Clinical Practice Guidelines for Management of Acute  Otitis Media in Children–2018 (the Guidelines 2018) are the  4th edition of the guidelines in Japan. Subcommittee on the  Guidelines published the first edition in 2006 to respond to  the increasing demand for the solution of the prevalence of  intractable acute otitis media (AOM) in children since the late  1990s in Japan. The aim of the Guidelines has been to pro-  vide appropriate recommendations about diagnosis and op-  timal management for the pediatric patients under 15 years  of age with acute otitis media. These evidence-based rec-  ommendations were created with the consensus of the sub-  committee members, taking into consideration unique charac-  teristics of bacteriology and antimicrobial susceptibilities of  AOM pathogens in Japan. The first revision was made in 2009  mainly to improve the assessment method of disease severity  and to reflect that on the treatment algorithm. The 3rd edition  introduced new treatment algorithm with new oral antimicro-  bial agents for intractable acute otitis media in 2013.

The Guidelines 2018 have included the clinical questions  and the recommendations about recurrent acute otitis media  (recurrent AOM) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, by  which routine vaccination has started in April 2013 in Japan.  Furthermore, this edition is the first one that has adopted the  AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) method, which has  been widely used in several guidelines in recent years, for  the evaluation of the evidence quality and strength of the  recommendation.

We have proposed the guidelines for disease severity-based  management of AOM patients, after classifying AOM severity  into mild, moderate, and severe, based on age, clinical man-  ifestations, and otoscopic findings. Precise otoscopic findings  are essential for judging AOM severity, which can lead to  appropriate management of AOM patients.

A B S T R A C T

In this study, a novel Quantum Self-Attention Neural Network for Multi-Model Aerial Image Classification  (QSANN-MAIC) is proposed. The objective of this paper is to develop a high-performance learning framework  capable of accurately classifying UAV-acquired aerial images. Initially, the proposed QSANN-MAIC model pre-  processes the input images through several enhancement steps, including noise reduction, sharpening,  contrast enhancement, and color correction, to eliminate unwanted distortions and improve image clarity for  further analysis. We have used a multi-model feature extraction framework to obtain rich and complementary  feature representations, integrating three architectures: a compact Vision Transformer, an enhanced ConvNeXt  model, and a fine-tuned VGG16 network. Subsequently, a quantum self-attention neural network is utilized to  perform the final classification by effectively capturing long-range dependencies among the extracted features.  To validate the effectiveness of the proposed QSANN-MAIC model, extensive simulations are conducted and  evaluated using multiple performance metrics. Comparative analysis demonstrates that the QSANN-MAIC  approach achieves improved performance across several evaluation measures.
1. Introduction

In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have attracted  significant attention across various fields, including mobile relaying,  surveillance, data acquisition, and monitoring. UAVs are capable of  providing line-of-sight (LoS) communication links, which enhances  connectivity and improves the reliability of communication systems [1].  Owing to their relatively low cost, high mobility, and flexible deploy­ ment capabilities, UAVs have been widely adopted for numerous ap­ plications such as search and rescue missions, precision agriculture,  disaster monitoring, and early environmental observation [2]. Further­ more, UAVs can function as mobile relay platforms to extend network  coverage and improve communication capacity. With the rapid growth  of the information technology (IT) sector, researchers are increasingly  focusing on utilizing UAVs to provide global internet access, particularly  for users located in remote or hard-to-reach areas [3]. UAV-based sys­ tems also create an aerial communication environment that is highly  suitable for wireless transmission, as they can deliver wireless signals to  ground users in regions experiencing network congestion or lacking  sufficient terrestrial infrastructure [4].

Within UAV-based applications, land cover (LC) classification  plays a crucial role; however, developing a fully automated and reliable  classification system remains a challenging task. Aerial scene image  classification involves categorizing captured aerial imagery into  different subclasses in order to represent various ground objects and  land cover (LC) categories, which often consist of numerous semantic  classes [5]. In many practical remote sensing (RS) applications, such as  resource management, urban planning, and computer-based cartog­ raphy, aerial image classification plays a significant role [6]. Typically,  several related object categories or LC types may appear across different  scene types. For example, both residential and commercial areas may  contain common elements such as buildings, roads, and trees; however,  they differ in terms of spatial arrangement and density distribution of  these components [7]. As a result, identifying aerial scenes based on  their structural characteristics and spatial patterns remains a chal­ lenging task [8].

To overcome the challenges of limited feature diversity, intricate  aerial scene structures, and uneven image quality in UAV-based aerial  image classification, this article proposes a QSANN-MAIC system. The  proposed QSANN-MAIC model follows a multi-faceted approach for  attaining the effective classification of aerial images, encompassing  preprocessing, multi-model feature representation, and a quantum  attention based classification module. The assessment of the proposed  QSANN-MAIC model is performed under a benchmark dataset. The  following are the major contributions of this research:

• A novel QSANN-MAIC is proposed to address the challenges of  limited feature diversity, complex aerial scene structures, and vary­ ing image quality in UAV imagery. • A novel multi-model feature extraction framework is developed by  integrating compact vision transformer (ComViT), improved Con­ vNeXt, and fine-tuned VGG16. • Learn global structural patterns, hierarchical spatial details, and fine-  grained texture features simultaneously, which results in richer and  more discriminative representations. • Introduce a QSANN to capture long-range dependencies and complex  feature interactions, which improves model sensitivity toward subtle  variations in aerial scenes and enhancing classification accuracy. • Conduct extensive performance evaluation to validate the proposed  QSANN-MAIC model’s efficiency under diverse metrics and demon­ strate the betterment of the QSANN-MAIC system under the bench­ mark EuroSat Dataset.

The remainder of this manuscript is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a comprehensive literature review of existing studies on aerial  image classification techniques. Section 3 describes the proposed ar­ chitecture and workflow in detail, including the dataset employed,  image pre-processing methods, multi-model feature extraction tech­ niques, classification architectures, and the evaluation metrics used to  assess the performance of the QSANN-MAIC model. Section 4 presents  the experimental results along with comparative analysis and an abla­ tion study to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.  Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper by summarizing the key
contributions and findings of the study.
2. Mathematical models and system architecture

This study follows a structured approach for the efficient classifica­ tion of aerial images using UAV. Fig. 1 provides a high-level overview of  the research methodology adopted in this work. Benchmark EuroSat  Dataset serves as the foundation for model development and evaluation.  As depicted in Fig. 1, the proposed QSANN-MAIC system encompasses  preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification modules. First input  images are standardized through noise reduction, sharpening, contrast  improvement, and color correction, and are augmented during training  to improve robustness. Three complementary backbones: ComViT for  global context, an improved ConvNeXt for hierarchical spatial patterns,  and a fine-tuned VGG16 for low-level texture cues, which are employed  to capture diverse feature representations. Then, these extracted fea­ tures are integrated through a learned fusion mechanism to form a  compact, discriminative descriptor. The fused features are further  passed to a QSANN to model complex, long-range feature interactions  and produce the final classification.

1. Background

Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) is a chronic infection of the  middle ear with perforation of the tympanic membrane and secrete from  the ear for more than two months, either continuously or intermittently  [1]. According to WHO, the prevalence of CSOM in the world is 65–330  million people, with 60% of whom experiencing hearing loss. Mean­ while, the incidence rate is 9 cases out of 100,000 population [2]. The  high incidence of CSOM is influenced by the etiology and the patho­ genesis of the CSOM itself. There are several influencing factors, such as  infection, anatomy or physiology dysfunction, environment, allergy, or  patient’s factor including immunity, gender, and others [3]. Clinically,  CSOM is classified into two types, namely the tubotympanic and the  atticoantral. CSOM disease begins with inflammation of the middle ear  that lasts a long time and does not receive adequate management [3,4].

Symptoms of CSOM may include thick and stink discharge from the  ear canal (otorrhea), decreased hearing ability, ringing in ears, ear pain,  ear fullness, headache, and dizziness. Diagnosis of CSOM can be  confirmed by examination using an otoscope or a microscope, hearing  examination, facial nerve topography examination, bacterial culture

Ear canal cleaning (aural toilet) should be conducted using  warm normal saline or hydrogen peroxide 3% solution. The adminis­ tration of a broad-spectrum antibiotic to CSOM patients could be in form  of topical and systemical (orally or intravenously) for a minimum of 5  days to 2 weeks to eliminate CSOM without complications [2,4]. Patient  with treatment failure who presents with persistent otorrhea after three  weeks of treatment can be additionally treated with topical antibiotics  that are based on the culture in addition to the aural toilet. Oral treat­ ment can be given if there is no selection of topical therapeutics based on  the pathogen susceptibility pattern. Participants in this study were CSOM patients who underwent  treatment. Participant’s inclusion criteria were patients diagnosed with  CSOM [1,7,8]. Participant’s exclusion criteria included incomplete  participant medical records.

Abstract The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence techniques, particularly deep learning, has transformed medical imaging.  This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent research that leverage vision transformer (ViT) models for medical  image classification across various disciplines. The medical fields of focus include breast cancer, skin lesions, magnetic  resonance imaging brain tumors, lung diseases, retinal and eye analysis, COVID-19, heart diseases, colon cancer, brain dis- orders, diabetic retinopathy, skin diseases, kidney diseases, lymph node diseases, and bone analysis. Each work is critically  analyzed and interpreted with respect to its performance, data preprocessing methodologies, model architecture, transfer  learning techniques, model interpretability, and identified challenges. Our findings suggest that ViT shows promising results  in the medical imaging domain, often outperforming traditional convolutional neural networks (CNN). A comprehensive  overview is presented in the form of figures and tables summarizing the key findings from each field. This paper provides  critical insights into the current state of medical image classification using ViT and highlights potential future directions  for this rapidly evolving research area.
Keywords  Vision transformers · Medical image analysis · Convolutional neural networks · Medical image classification ·  Clinical decision support
Introduction

In a world where medical imaging serves as the linchpin of  modern diagnostics, harnessing the full potential of each  pixel can be a matter of life and death. Convolutional neu- ral networks, which are the main type of deep learning, have  already shown that they can change this field by getting to  levels of accuracy that have never been seen before, yet as  we stand on the brink of a new era, vision transformers are  revolutionizing the field, challenging conventional wisdom  and setting new standards for performance [1–3]. One type  of deep learning model that is often used in computer vision  tasks is the CNN, which sorts images into groups and finds  objects in them, CNNs work by convolving the input image  with filters to extract local features and then aggregating  these features through pooling layers, CNNs, on the other  hand, have flaws, like features that are only available in set  sizes and the failure to record world context information well  [4–8]. ViTs are a new type of deep neural networks that have  shown promise as an option to CNNs for picture-taking tasks;  ViTs are inspired by the transformer architecture originally  introduced for natural language processing (NLP) tasks. transformer design is based on self-attention processes that let  the network decide on the fly how important each trait in the  input chain is and gather information about the overall context  [3, 9]. This makes ViTs well suited for image analysis tasks  where global context information is important [10]. Vision  transformers work by converting an input image into a set of  fixed-length feature representations, also known as tokens,  the image is divided into non-overlapping square patches, and  each patch is treated as an individual feature. The tokens are  then processed through multi-head self-attention mechanisms,  which dynamically weigh the importance of each token in  the input sequence. This allows the network to capture global  context information and focus on different parts of the image  based on the context [6, 10]. ViTs’ main parts are tokeniza- tion, self-sttention mechanisms, feed-forward networks, and  pooling and classification layers [11]. Tokenization in vision  transformers is the process of breaking down a picture into  a set of fixed-length feature representations, also known as  tokens, which can be processed by a transformer-based model.  This is typically done by encoding the image into a multi- dimensional feature map and then flattening this map into a  one-dimensional vector, this vector is then passed through a  linear layer to produce the final set of token representations.  Tokenization is a necessary preprocessing step in vision trans- formers because it lets the model work with pictures. Self- attention mechanisms are a key component in the architecture  of vision transformers, which are neural networks designed  to process visual information, in self-attention, each element  in a sequence (e.g., an image) attends to every other element  in that sequence, weighing its importance in the computa- tion of the final representation. This allows the network to  dynamically focus on different parts of the image based on  context and capture long-range dependencies [12]. In vision  transformers, self-attention is applied over the spatial dimen- sions of the image, rather than the temporal dimension as in  traditional transformer models. The result is a more power- ful and efficient network that can handle large and complex  images and is well suited for a variety of computer vision  tasks, including image classification and object detection.  Feed-forward networks (FFNs) are another key component  in the architecture of vision transformers, which are neural  networks designed to process visual information. FFNs are  used to transform the intermediate representations produced  by the self-attention mechanisms into a final output. The FFN  consists of a series of linear transformations followed by non- linear activation functions and can be thought of as a dense  layer in a traditional convolutional neural network. In vision  transformers, the FFN is typically used to map the high- dimensional representations produced by the self-attention  layers to a lower-dimensional space, suitable for the final pre- diction task (e.g., image classification). Vision transformers  can get more accurate results when they use both self-atten- tion and FFN layers together. This is because they can take

in both global and local information in a picture. The pooling  layer and the classification layer are used for down sampling  and final prediction in vision transformers, the pooling layer  is typically applied after the transformer blocks to reduce the  spatial resolution of the feature maps, this helps to reduce  the computational complexity and increase the robustness of  the model to small translations, common pooling operations  include max-pooling and average pooling. The classification  layer is a fully connected layer with a SoftMax activation used  to make the final prediction, the inputs to the classification  layer are the flattened feature maps obtained after pooling, and  the outputs are the class probabilities, the number of outputs  is equal to the number of classes in the classification task.  Together, the pooling and classification layers make up the  last part of a vision transformer’s prediction process. They  take a picture as input and make a guess about the things that  are in it. CNNs and ViTs are two popular architectures for  computer vision tasks such as image classification. ViTs have  been applied to a wide array of computer vision tasks, dem- onstrating their versatility and efficacy. They have achieved  state-of-the-art performance in image classification on bench- mark datasets such as ImageNet. In object detection, they have  incorporated object-level attention mechanisms, effectively  transforming the challenge into a token-level classification  problem. Additionally, ViTs have made strides in image  segmentation by implementing segmentation-specific atten- tion mechanisms, further showcasing their adaptability and  potential. The main difference between vision transformers  and CNNs lies in their architecture and how they process the  input image. CNNs extract local features through convolution  and pooling operations and are limited by their reliance on  fixed-sized local features. On the other hand, vision transform- ers use self-attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh the  importance of each feature in the input sequence, allowing  them to effectively capture global context information [4, 6,  13, 14]. Another difference between ViTs and CNNs is the  way they handle large images, CNNs typically use pooling  layers to reduce the spatial dimension of the input, which can  result in the loss of essential information. Vision transformers,  on the other hand, use self-attention mechanisms to dynami- cally focus on distinct parts of the image, making them well  suited for handling large images.

While several review papers have examined the role of  vision transformers in medical imaging, most existing sur- veys focus on general architectural discussions or applica- tions within a limited set of medical tasks, lacking a compre- hensive disease-centric perspective. This paper distinguishes  itself by adopting a structured, application-driven approach,  categorizing studies based on specific medical conditions  such as breast cancer classification, skin lesion analysis,  MRI brain tumor analysis, lung diseases, and retinal disor- ders. By systematically grouping research based on medical  application areas rather than a general technical perspective,

Abstract Purpose: To improve the explainability of a YOLOv5-based model for anterior segment disease diagnosis by combining  gradient-weighted class activation mapping ++ (Grad-CAM++) and cut-and-paste validation and evaluate the influence of  extracorneal information on diagnostic accuracy. Methods: In total, 1039 slit-lamp photographs across nine diagnostic categories were analyzed using a previously developed  YOLOv5 model. Grad-CAM++ was implemented to visualize the attention patterns across key network layers. To quantita- tively assess clinical relevance, attention maps were compared against expert-delineated lesion boundaries using Intersection  over Union (IoU). Furthermore, cut-and-paste validation was performed by systematically swapping the corneal regions with  different backgrounds to probe the reliance of the model on contextual information. Results: Grad-CAM++ analysis revealed hierarchical attention focus, progressing from broad in the early layers to highly  localized in the final layers, with layer 23 showing distinct disease-specific patterns. Cut-and-paste validation demonstrated  that model accuracy was highly dependent on the background context for certain diseases; for instance, the accuracy for  infectious keratitis and acute primary angle closure dropped significantly upon background alteration. Critically, the clinical  relevance of the attention maps measured by the IoU against expert annotations was significantly higher for correct predic- tions than for incorrect predictions, linking the model’s visual explanation to its diagnostic reliability. Conclusion: Combining Grad-CAM++ with cut-and-paste validation provided a robust framework for evaluating the explain- ability of the YOLOv5 model. This dual approach reveals layer-specific attention dynamics and quantifies the model’s  reliance on clinically relevant extracorneal features, thereby enhancing the transparency and trustworthiness of artificial  intelligence-based diagnostic systems in ophthalmology.

Introduction

Anterior segment diseases are a leading cause of prevent- able blindness worldwide, with conditions such as infectious  keratitis affecting millions of people annually, warranting  prompt and accurate diagnosis for preventing vision loss.  The complexity of the anterior segment pathology, rang- ing from subtle corneal infiltrates to diffuse inflammatory  patterns, poses significant diagnostic challenges even for  experienced ophthalmologists. This diagnostic complexity  has driven the development of artificial intelligence (AI)

systems to assist in clinical decision-making. Recent deep  learning models have demonstrated remarkable performance  in the detection of various anterior segment conditions, such  as infectious keratitis [1–5], herpes keratitis [6], pterygium  [7], eyelid tumors [8, 9], allergic conjunctivitis [10], and  cataracts [11, 12].

However, the clinical adoption of these high-performing  AI models faces a critical barrier: a lack of interpretability  in their decision-making processes. While models have dem- onstrated impressive accuracy metrics, with some achieving  superhuman performance in differentiating fungal keratitis  from bacterial keratitis (area under the curve [AUC] up to  0.99) [1, 4–7]—clinicians remain reluctant to trust black-box  Extended author information available on the last page of the article

systems whose reasoning cannot be examined. This concern  is particularly acute in ophthalmology, where subtle visual  cues guide treatment decisions and misdiagnosis can lead to  irreversible vision loss. More troublingly, recent evidence  suggests that many medical AI models achieve high accuracy  through “shortcut learning,” exploiting spurious correlations  rather than learning clinically relevant features [13, 14]. For  instance, neuroimaging models have been shown to identify  MRI scanner types with 96% accuracy using hardware sig- natures rather than anatomical features, with performance  dropping to chance levels when these confounders were  removed [13].

Current approaches to AI interpretability in anterior seg- ment imaging primarily rely on gradient-based visualiza- tion methods, particularly Gradient-weighted Class Activa- tion Mapping (Grad-CAM) [15]. Although Grad-CAM has  been widely adopted to highlight the regions of interest in  corneal images [1, 4–7], significant limitations compro- mise its clinical utility. First, Grad-CAM often produces  coarse, inconsistent localizations that may not align with  expert-identified pathological regions [16–18]. Second,  when applied to complex object detection architectures,  such as YOLO, which is increasingly used for multidisease  classification, the question of which network layer provides  clinically meaningful explanations remains unresolved  [19–22]. Third, and most critically, visualization methods  alone cannot determine whether models rely on appropri- ate clinical features or spurious contextual cues [23]. For  example, for infectious keratitis, a model may correctly  classify cases by detecting conjunctival hyperemia (a sec- ondary sign) rather than primary corneal pathology. This  could lead to misdiagnosis in two scenarios: missing early  infections that lack inflammatory signs, or incorrect diag- nosis of non-infectious conditions with hyperemia, such as  infectious keratitis.

These limitations necessitate a more comprehensive  approach to model validation. Therefore, this study aimed  to establish a framework for evaluating the explainability  and clinical reliability of AI models for anterior segment  disease diagnosis by implementing a novel two-stage  validation approach based on a previously developed  YOLOv5 model [12]. The first stage addresses the known  limitations of standard Grad-CAM, which can produce  coarse or inconsistent localizations [16–18]. To achieve  more refined attention maps, this study employs Grad- CAM++, an enhanced method that incorporates second- order gradients for more precise weighting and improved  localization [24–27]. While comparative studies have  demonstrated mixed results, with Grad-CAM++ strug- gling with smaller lesions in other domains [28], its effec- tiveness for larger, well-defined pathologies typical in  anterior segment imaging was assessed here. The second  stage employs “cut-and-paste” validation—systematically

altering image contexts to directly test the model’s fea- ture dependence [29]. This technique probes whether the  model relies on primary pathological features or poten- tially misleading contextual cues, such as conjunctival  injection, which represent both clinically relevant infor- mation and a potential source of diagnostic bias. By com- bining these complementary methods, this study aimed to  answer three critical questions: (1) Which network layers  provide the most clinically interpretable explanations?  (2) To what extent do the models rely on corneal pathol- ogy versus the extracorneal context? (3) Can visualization  quality metrics predict diagnostic reliability? Answering  these questions is essential for developing trustworthy AI  systems that can safely augment clinical decision making  in ophthalmology.
Materials and Methods
Ethical Approval

This study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Review  Board of the Japanese Ophthalmological Society (protocol  number: 15000133–20001) and included 23 tertiary univer- sity hospitals. All the procedures followed the tenets of the  Declaration of Helsinki and the Japanese Guidelines for Life  Science and Medical Research. In view of the retrospective  design, the requirement for written informed consent was  waived and an opt-out approach was implemented, allow- ing patients to decline participation through an institutional  website.
Study Design

This study evaluated the interpretability of a deep learn- ing model based on the YOLOv5 architecture, previously  trained on a dataset of 5270 anterior segment photographs  from 5270 individual patients obtained using diffuse illu- mination through a multi-institutional collaborative net- work. The dataset was collected from 15 tertiary referral  centers across Japan. The model was designed to classify  the anterior segment conditions into nine categories: nor- mal, infectious keratitis, non-infectious keratitis, scar,  tumor, deposit, acute primary angle closure (APAC), lens  opacity, and bullous keratopathy. Standardized image  acquisition protocols and diagnostic criteria were applied  across all participating centers to ensure data consistency  and quality.

For this interpretability analysis, 1039 slit-lamp photo- graphs encompassing all nine diagnostic categories were  used: normal (258), infectious keratitis (129), non-infec- tious keratitis (71), scar (140), tumor (176), deposit (123),  APAC (11), lens opacity (68), and bullous keratopathy (63).

To prevent potential bias,  duplicate images from the same patient or condition were  excluded. Furthermore, a preliminary inference using the  YOLOv5 model confirmed an accuracy of 85%, which is  consistent with previously reported results (Fig. S1) [12].
YOLOv5 Model

YOLOv5 consists of three main architectural components:  the backbone, neck, and head networks. Each component  serves a distinct function within the object detection pipe- line and works together to enable efficient and accurate  detection (Fig. 1) [30].

The backbone network functions primarily as a fea- ture extractor by utilizing a cross-stage partial network  architecture. Its core component, the C3 module, splits  the input features into two paths: one processes informa- tion through multiple bottleneck layers, whereas the other  directly dispatches the features. This dual-path structure  reduces computational complexity while preserving essen- tial feature information. Moreover, the backbone incorpo- rates a spatial pyramid pooling module in its final stage. The C3 module was integrated throughout the network  to enhance feature processing. Each module includes a  1 × 1 convolution layer that splits the input features into  two branches: one processes the features through multiple  residual blocks, whereas the other bypasses these opera- tions. The outputs from both branches were subsequently  concatenated and refined through a final 1 × 1 convolu- tion layer, effectively combining local and global feature  information.

In the neck network, YOLOv5 utilizes a bidirectional fea- ture pyramid architecture that integrates a feature pyramid  network and path aggregation network. The feature pyra- mid network propagates semantically rich features from the  higher to lower feature maps, whereas the path aggregation  network transmits spatially precise localization features from  the lower to higher feature maps. This dual-path structure  enhances feature fusion across different network layers,  thereby improving overall detection performance.

A key feature of YOLOv5 is its three prediction Heads,  which operate at different scales to enable multiscale object  detection. The first prediction head processes 80× 80 × 256  feature maps to detect large objects (Layer 17). The second  Head processes 40× 40 × 512 feature maps for medium- sized objects (Layer 20), whereas the third Head processes  20× 20 × 1024 feature maps for small objects (Layer 23).  Each prediction head generated an output channel containing  detection information, including object center coordinates,  bounding box dimensions, object presence probability, and  class probabilities, through a Conv2D layer (layers 24–0,  24–1, and 24–2). In YOLOv5, the likelihood calculation uses a sigmoid  function to compute the prediction scores. For a feature  value xb,c in the final layer, the predictive score sb,c is calcu- lated as sb,c = 1 1+e−xb,c , where b represents the index of the  estimated bounding boxes and c represents the category  index. This calculation normalized the prediction scores  between 0 and 1, with the highest-scoring category selected  as the final classification result.
YOLOv5‐Grad‐CAM and YOLOv5‐Grad‐CAM++

Grad-CAM++ was employed to effectively visualize the  model attention patterns within the multiscale architecture  of YOLOv5. This method enhances the visualization of the  attention regions, particularly in models with complex net- work structures, such as YOLOv5. This approach focuses on  two key stages, feature processing and final prediction, and  provides a comprehensive understanding of the decision- making process of the model.

The first set of the Grad-CAM++ layers was implemented  immediately before the 17_cv3_conv, 20_cv3_conv, and 23_ cv3_conv layers, which corresponded to the convolutional  layers of the final C3 modules (layers 17, 20, and 23, respec- tively). These layers processed information-rich features on  multiple spatial scales (80 × 80 × 256, 40 × 40 × 512, and  20 × 20 × 1024, respectively). The second set was positioned  immediately before the 24_m_0, 24_m_1, and 24_m_2 lay- ers, which served as the final prediction convolutional layers  (layers 24–0, 24–1, and 24–2, respectively), where the model  performed its final detection and classification decisions.  This dual-layer placement strategy, with visualization lay- ers positioned directly before the key convolutional layers,  made it possible to track how the network processed and  transformed the features throughout its architecture (Fig. 1).  These layer names follow the official YOLOv5 implementa- tion [31].

The Grad-CAM++ computation followed a systematic  approach. First, the gradients were calculated with respect  to the target class for each activation map. These gradients  undergo global average pooling to generate channel-wise  importance weights, which are then used to create weighted  combinations of the forward activation maps. Finally, a recti- fied linear unit activation function was applied to highlight  regions that positively contributed to model predictions [16].  Although Grad-CAM was initially implemented, the analysis  primarily focused on Grad-CAM++ owing to its superior  performance in localizing relevant features within complex  architectures.
Grad‐CAM++ Feature Analysis

To comprehensively evaluate the model performance,  attention patterns across all nine diagnostic categories  were analyzed using Grad-CAM++ visualizations. As  outlined in the previous section, the analysis primarily  focused on layer 23, which was presumed to capture the  most relevant scale features for corneal lesion detection.  Attention maps were generated at three network depths  corresponding to the detection scales of the model and  normalized to a range of 0–1. To facilitate visual inter- pretation, these maps were color coded using a continuous  spectrum, with blue and red representing the lowest and  highest attention, respectively.

The analysis examined both the qualitative and quanti- tative aspects of attention patterns. A qualitative compari- son between Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++ visualizations  was first performed, revealing that Grad-CAM++ pro- vided a more precise and clinically relevant localization  of the attention regions, particularly in layer 23. Cut‐and‐Paste Validation

To determine whether the extracorneal information influ- enced the classification decisions of the model, a cut-and- paste validation approach was used. From the full data- set of 1039 images, a subset of 341 images meeting the  following criteria was selected to serve as background  templates: minimal eyelid overlap, correct model classifi- cation, and a predictive score exceeding 90%. The distribu- tions of the selected backgrounds were as follows: normal
(n = 66), tumor (n = 64), deposit (n = 60), infectious kera- titis (n = 50), scar (n = 40), bullous keratopathy (n = 23),  noninfectious keratitis (n = 20), lens opacity (n = 12), and  APAC (n = 6).

For corneal extraction and replacement, CVAT annota- tion software (Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, USA) was  used to annotate the corneal regions with elliptical approx- imations, recording the center coordinates, major axis,  and minor axis of each cornea. Using these annotations,  a Python-based pipeline was developed to extract the 341  corneal regions from background images and systematically  replace the cornea in each of the 341 background templates.  To ensure proper fitting, the extracted corneas were scaled  along their major and minor axes to match the dimensions  of the corneal region of the target background, thereby gen- erating approximately 116,000 composite images for the  analysis (Fig. 3).

Background: Ear and mastoid disease can easily be treated by early detection and appropriate medical care. How- ever, short of specialists and relatively low diagnostic accuracy calls for a new way of diagnostic strategy, in which deep learning may play a significant role. The current study presents a machine learning model to automatically diagnose ear disease using a large database of otoendoscopic images acquired in the clinical environment. Methods: Total 10,544 otoendoscopic images were used to train nine public convolution-based deep neural net- works to classify eardrum and external auditory canal features into six categories of ear diseases, covering most ear diseases (Normal, Attic retraction, Tympanic perforation, Otitis externa±myringitis, Tumor). Findings: According to accuracy and training time, transfer learning models based on Inception-V3 and ResNet101 were chosen and the ensemble classifier using the two models yielded a significant improvement over each model, the accuracy of which is in average 93·67% for the 5-folds cross-validation. Considering sub- stantial data-size dependency of classifier performance in the transfer learning, evaluated in this study, the high accuracy in the current model is attributable to the large database. Interpretation: The current study is unprecedented in terms of both disease diversity and diagnostic accuracy, which is compatible or even better than an average otolaryngologist. The classifier was trained with data in a var- ious acquisition condition, which is suitable for the practical environment. This study shows the usefulness of uti- lizing a deep learning model in the early detection and treatment of ear disease in the clinical situation. 1. Introduction

Ear and mastoid disease (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD) code H.60-H.95) is a com- mon disease that can easily be treated with early medical care. Never- theless, if one does not receive timely detection and appropriate

treatment, it may leave sequelae, such as hearing impairment. In the evaluation of ear and mastoid disease in the clinic, physical examination using conventional otoscopy or otoendoscopy as well as history taking is the first step. However, diagnosis by non-otolaryngologists using otoscopy or otoendoscopy is highly susceptible to misdiagnosis [1]. In a study by Pichichero, Poole [2], the correct diagnosis rate of otitis media diagnosed by 514 pediatricians using pneumatic otoscope was an average rate of 50%. The study also shows a higher (compared to pe- diatricians) but not a satisfactory accuracy of 73% when diagnosed by 188 otolaryngologists. This low diagnostic accuracy implies that diagno- sis of ear disease without the help of additional resources such as imag- ing or acoustic testing is difficult even for specialists. The short of specialists in the local clinic and their relatively low diagnostic accuracy calls for a new way of diagnostic strategy, in which machine learning may play a significant role.

As far as we know, relatively few machine learning studies have been conducted for automated diagnosis of ear disease using otoscopic images. Myburgh and colleagues reported auto-diagnosis of otitis media, with an accuracy of 81·58% by decision tree and 86·84% by neu- ral network method [3], which conducted a classification of tympanic membrane into five groups between normal eardrum, otitis media with perforation, acute otitis media, otitis media with effusion and ceru- men impaction. However, the classification categories lack important and critical diagnosis such as attic retraction.

For clinical use, the current study is conducted to provide a reliable diagnosis of otitis media, attic retraction, atelectasis, tumors, and otitis externa, using deep learning for otoscopy photos of the eardrum and ex- ternal auditory canal (EAC). These categories cover most of the domain of ear diseases that could be diagnosed using otoendoscopy in the clinics. For this, we proposed an ensemble classifier of two best- performing deep neural networks evaluated for ear images.

Deep learning or deep neural network has been introduced to vari- ous fields of medicine successfully. For example, in the field of ophthal- mology, the machine learning result is comparable to a level of specialist [4–6]. Most of these studies utilize convolutional neural network (CNN),

a supervised deep learning method. However, building CNN from scratch requires a large amount of dataset and computational power, which is not practical in many application areas. Instead, public CNN models pretrained for natural images could be reused and fine-tuned to a specific application, which is called transfer learning. In transfer learning, most network layers in a public network model are transferred to a new model, followed by a new fully-connected layer that classifies those features into a new set of classes. Studies with transfer learning for medical imaging showed high classification accuracy comparable to, or even better to building CNN from scratch [7,8].

This study is composed of the following three main parts. First, we evaluated the performance of nine public models to choose the best models in terms of accuracy and training time for the current applica- tion. Based on this evaluation, ensemble classifier to combine multiple models' classification results was proposed, which is expected to in- crease the overall classification performance than using a single classi- fier. Second, although transfer learning is known to be efficient in a relatively small dataset (as in labelled medical images), the dependency of the classification accuracy and model type on the size of the dataset is not exampled yet. Thus, we tested the performance of the classifier de- pending on the data size. We also conducted optimization of the model configuration, by assigning a hidden layer in the fully connected net- work layer, and changing colour channels in the image database. Finally, we showed and discussed the characteristics of the proposed model for diagnosing ear diseases in the clinical setting.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Patient selection and data acquisition

Data from patients who visited the outpatient clinic in Severance Hospital otorhinolaryngology department from the year 2013 to 2017 were used. As a routine, patients had their otoendoscopic photo taken upon visit. Drum photos were taken with either 4 mm or 2.7 mm OTOLUX 0-degree telescope (MGB Endoskopische Geräte GmbH Berlin, Germany) tethered to Olympus OTV-SP1 video imaging system (Olym- pus Corporation, Japan), by otolaryngology residents, faculty or experi- enced nurses. The image resolution was 640 by 480 pixels. A total of 19,496 endoscope photos were reviewed for labelling. Since otoendoscopic findings of post-surgery status are mostly subjective and rely on the surgeon, 7602 photos were excluded. Additionally, 1350 photos were excluded since the photos were not appropriate for examination, for example, sites not related to eardrum or EAC, dupli- cates, the picture was significantly blurred due to handshakes or focus problems, or the author could not agree despite attending physician's medical records, acoustic and radiologic test results. Since photos were taken by several clinicians, and the external auditory canal is sub- ject to individual variation, the composition of photography was not standardized; colour arrangements, white balance, eardrum size, loca- tion, rotation, angle, and light reflection in images were variable, but the photo was analyzed as-is to reflect real-life clinical setting. Research in context
Evidence before this study

Ear and mastoid disease is a common disease, which demands early and appropriate diagnosis with otoscopy or otoendoscopy, but is not trivial in local clinics and the diagnosis rate even by oto- laryngologists using ear images show an unsatisfactory accuracy, as low as 73%. So far, the best known study for automatic diag- nosis of ear disease using images has been done with tympanic membrane using a shallow neural network of relatively small data size (n ~ 390) with an accuracy of 86.84%, however, the previous method is only capable of partially diagnosing middle ear disease.
Added value of this study

This is the first study to utilize a deep learning scheme to classify tympanic membrane otoendoscopic images into six diagnostic categories, especially including attic retractions and tumors, using a large database (n = 10,544), and the deep learning model covers most of the ear diseases in the clinic, not only on the middle ear but also on the external ear. The ensemble classifier, which we propose, shows better performance than using a single transferred deep learning model with an accuracy of 93·67%.

According to our evaluation on the relationship between database size and the performance of the transfer deep learning models, current study suggests the need for a sufficient size of the data- base for a reliable classification performance in the medical image domain. Abstract
Objectives: To summarise the accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI) computer vision
algorithms to classify ear disease from otoscopy.
Design: Systematic review and meta-­analysis.
Methods: Using the PRISMA guidelines, nine online databases were searched for articles
that used AI computer vision algorithms developed from various methods (convolutional
neural networks, artificial neural networks, support vector machines, decision trees and
k-­nearest neighbours) to classify otoscopic images. Diagnostic classes of interest: normal
tympanic membrane, acute otitis media (AOM), otitis media with effusion (OME), chronic
otitis media (COM) with or without perforation, cholesteatoma and canal obstruction.
Main outcome measures: Accuracy to correctly classify otoscopic images compared
to otolaryngologists (ground truth). The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy
Studies Version 2 tool was used to assess the quality of methodology and risk of bias.
Results: Thirty-­nine articles were included. Algorithms achieved 90.7% (95%CI:
90.1–­91.3%) accuracy to difference between normal or abnormal otoscopy images
in 14 studies. The most common multiclassification algorithm (3 or more diagnostic
classes) achieved 97.6% (95%CI: 97.3–­97.9%) accuracy to differentiate between nor-
mal, AOM and OME in three studies. AI algorithms outperformed human assessors to
classify otoscopy images achieving 93.4% (95%CI: 90.5–­96.4%) versus 73.2% (95%CI:
67.9–­78.5%) accuracy in three studies. Convolutional neural networks achieved the
highest accuracy compared to other classification methods.
Conclusion: AI can classify ear disease from otoscopy. A concerted effort is required
to establish a comprehensive and reliable otoscopy database for algorithm training.
An AI-­supported otoscopy system may assist health care workers, trainees and pri-
mary care practitioners with less otology experience identify ear disease.

ABSTRACT Diagnosing ear diseases from images of the tympanic membrane has emerged as a promising  application for deep learning-based classification models. While several studies report high diagnostic  accuracy, these models often struggle to generalize to external data that does not match the image  characteristics of the training data. This study aims to evaluate methods for enhancing model generalizability.  We trained artificial neural networks on tympanic membrane images from five datasets with a large  heterogeneity between them. The datasets consisted of images from different countries, captured with  different otoscope models, and with different image pre-processing applied at the source (e.g., colour  normalization, cropping, and resolution). Artificial neural networks for binary (normal/abnormal)  classification were trained on three datasets, and the models were evaluated on two. We explored several  strategies to improve generalizability, including image pre-processing, data augmentation, transfer learning,  and different network architectures. The effects of each investigated factor and their interactions were  determined through a full factorial experimental design and linear mixed-effects model. Our best  classification network achieved a mean accuracy of 83% (sensitivity 71%, specificity 91%) on external  datasets. In contrast, the baseline trained without an optimized training method and using non-processed  datasets yielded an accuracy of 53% (sensitivity 83%, specificity 34%). Our findings highlight how a better  choice of network, training and augmentation strategies, and data verification improve model generalizability.

I. INTRODUCTION  Globally, one in five people live with hearing loss, and  most of them lack access to interventions [1]. Many of these  cases are preventable with early detection and treatment. In  pediatric care, a very common diagnosis is acute otitis  media (AOM), which may need antibiotic treatment to  avoid severe complications. In underserved areas, where  there are few specialists available to diagnose ear diseases,  there is a need for new diagnostic tools that do not require  specialist knowledge or expensive equipment. This is one  of the motivations for developing computer vision-based  diagnostic support systems.  Computer vision models can be used for the classification  of ear diseases from images of the tympanic membrane

(TM; Figure 1) taken by simple digital otoscopes. In the last  years several studies have shown that using deep learning  (DL) methods such as convolutional neural networks  (CNNs) for the identification of different ear diseases can  outperform general practitioners when using only an image  of the ear drum as input [2]. However, there are several

A first challenge is the reproducibility of earlier DL  methods, which is often constrained by inadequate  documentation of model implementation and training  hyperparameters, or the use of proprietary datasets [3].  Another issue is the generalizability of machine learning  (ML) models. Model accuracies can be very high on test  sets derived from the training data, but when the model  encounters  new  input  that  does  not  match  the  characteristics of the training data, accuracy often drops  considerably [4]. This phenomenon is known as dataset or  domain shift and has many possible causes [5]. Domain  shift is a well-known issue in medical image classification,  and presents in the form of either covariate shift caused by  changes in image characteristics, or concept shift caused by  inter-rater variability [6]. It is not reasonable to be able to  anticipate and compensate for all possible future shifts in  the data distribution when the domain is as complex and  high-dimensional as medical images. In practice it is more  common to manually monitor a deployed ML system to  identify changes in the input or decreasing model accuracy  to update the model when needed, but ideally the system  should be as robust as possible to these changes [4]. Despite  that, in the recent literature, we have observed the rise of

foundation models, which have shown promise in  addressing the challenges posed by shifts in data  distribution, particularly in complex, high-dimensional  domains like medical imaging [7]. These models are trained  on extensive and diverse datasets, enabling them to learn  generalizable representations that can capture variations  across a wide range of input scenarios. This foundational  knowledge can allow them to handle new, unseen data  distributions more effectively than traditional models,  thereby reducing the frequency and extent of manual  intervention needed post-deployment.  DL methods using large neural networks typically perform  better when it comes to generalization as compared to  traditional ML, but because of their high capacity, they also  tend to over-fit to less general characteristics or biases of  the training data. Training a deep neural network (DNN) to  generalize well and achieve good accuracy requires a large  amount of data that captures as much variability in the  domain as possible [8].  In medical applications, data scarcity becomes a problem  because acquiring new data is costly, and data sharing is  subject to privacy concerns and ethics review approval. In  the case of tympanic membrane images taken by digital  otoscope/endoscope, there are currently only three publicly  available datasets published, each covering a different set  of ear conditions [9], [10], [11]. A recent study showed that  when training an image classifier on one of these three  datasets and then evaluating its performance on one of the  others, the accuracy was severely reduced [12]. This result  agrees with previous considerations, and it can be  understood intuitively by looking at the visual difference  between the samples in the datasets given the use of  different otoscopes, subject demographics, and image  preprocessing techniques employed. It was then shown that  training a model on all three datasets will improve accuracy  on a test set from any of the individual datasets, which is  expected when the training and test data are from similar  distributions [12]. Although this shows the benefit of  having as much varied data as possible, a limitation is that  it does not tell us how good the model will perform on  future data with another unknown dataset shift.  Recent work has also examined biases within these specific  datasets. Xu et al. [13] systematically analyzed the same  three public datasets used here for training (Türkiye, Chile,  and Ohio/USA) and showed, through counterfactual  masking and color-feature experiments, that classifiers can  achieve high internal performance by exploiting non- clinical artifacts (illumination, color saturation, image  framing, and near-duplicate images) rather than clinically  meaningful features. This shows the importance of both the  data-quality review and the strict external-dataset  evaluation used in this study.  Cross-dataset generalization and benchmarking have  received growing attention in the medical image  classification literature. Matta et al. [6] reviewed

The  present study builds on this by applying a structured  experimental design to quantify the relative importance of  several generalization-improving strategies in the otoscopy  domain.  The aim of this study was to investigate different methods  to improve model generalizability (without having more  data) when using a DNN-based image classifier for  detecting abnormal tympanic membranes. For this task we  added two additional TM image repositories [14], [15], [16]  in addition to the three above-mentioned datasets for a  wider representation of domain shifts. To pursue this goal,  we identified three sub-aims. The first was to show the  problem of using a single source of data, and the difference  an improved model training approach can make. The  second aim was to compare the importance of which neural  network architecture is used in relation to the different  generalizability-improving methods applied when training  the network. The final aim was to quantify the effects and  interactions of several different generalizability-improving  methods through statistical methods, to understand which  are the most effective and if there are synergistic effects.  For the second and third aim we used the first three datasets  to train the model and used the last two as an external test  set with a considerable domain shift.  The main contributions of this study are: (1) a systematic  empirical  evaluation  of  multiple  generalizability- improving methods across five heterogeneous tympanic  membrane image datasets with substantial domain shift; (2)  a full factorial experimental design enabling statistical  quantification of the main effects and interaction effects of  network architecture, training method, augmentation  strategy, and data quality on cross-dataset performance;  and (3) a publicly available implementation of the  optimized training pipeline to facilitate reproducibility.  While the individual methods are not novel in isolation,  their systematic comparison in a cross-dataset medical  imaging context, and the resulting guidance on which  factors matter most, constitutes the primary contribution of  this work.

II. METHODS  A. GENERALIZABILITY-IMPROVING METHODS IN DEEP  LEARNING  1) TRANSFER LEARNING  Transfer learning refers to using a model trained on a  separate task as a starting point. In the image classification  domain, it is very common to use models pre-trained on the  large-scale ImageNet database [17]. Since ImageNet is  orders of magnitude larger than most medical image datasets  it enables training large neural networks without overfitting,  so they learn efficient image feature extraction. This pre- trained model can either be used as a feature extractor, in

which  a new classification model is added and trained on the  output features, or alternatively training is continued with the  same model but on the new task. Transfer learning can  greatly speed up training of new models as well as improve  the model generalizability as it leverages knowledge of  similar tasks previously learned, when compared to training  from scratch [18]. The method of transfer learning used for  this study was “full fine-tuning", which means that none of  the learnable parameters of the pre-trained model were  frozen when training the model for the final task. This  approach was chosen as the optimal number of layers of a  pre-trained model to update is different depending on  network and dataset size and would require individual  adaptation for each tested network [19]. The potential for  overfitting is greater when training the full networks, but this  was compensated for with strong regularization.    2) REGULARIZATION  Current ML models are usually overparameterized meaning  they have a high capacity to overfit the training data. Such a  model can be trained to a point where the model perfectly  learns the samples used in training but does not perform well  on any new data. To avoid overfitting, there are many  different regularization methods applicable to deep learning  that aim to reduce unnecessary complexity in the model [20].  The regularization techniques used in this study were  dropout, batch normalization, stochastic depth, early  stopping, weight decay, label smoothing and data  augmentation.  Histogram equalization  as  a  dataset  preprocessing step was investigated but had a negative effect  on model performance (4.9% mean decrease in accuracy  across the thirteen tested networks compared to the baseline).    3) DATA AUGMENTATION  One of the primary techniques used in DL to avoid  overfitting and improve generalization is data augmentation  [21]. It is achieved by training a model using many copies of  each data sample with different small modifications. For  image classification models it is common to use geometric  transformations, color space adjustments and other image  distortions as augmentations. For this study we used the  automatic augmentation method TrivialAugment [22],  which randomly applies one of many different image  operations at a random strength to each sample. Of the  fourteen total augmentations that are sampled from, eleven  also has a strength, and three are binary choice. The  implementation of TrivialAugment used in the study is from  TorchVision, where details of each augmentation can be  found [23].    4) DEALING WITH NOISY LABELS  The “ground truth” of the TM images in the three public  datasets were all based on the classification of one or a few  otolaryngologists [9], [10], [11]. Since each dataset  contains a different set of pathologic ear conditions and we  want to evaluate models trained on any of them against any  of the others we divide each dataset into two groups: normal  and abnormal. ABSTRACT Diagnosing ear diseases from images of the tympanic membrane has emerged as a promising  application for deep learning-based classification models. While several studies report high diagnostic  accuracy, these models often struggle to generalize to external data that does not match the image  characteristics of the training data. This study aims to evaluate methods for enhancing model generalizability.  We trained artificial neural networks on tympanic membrane images from five datasets with a large  heterogeneity between them. Artificial neural networks for binary (normal/abnormal)  classification were trained on three datasets, and the models were evaluated on two. We explored several  strategies to improve generalizability, including image pre-processing, data augmentation, transfer learning,  and different network architectures. The effects of each investigated factor and their interactions were  determined through a full factorial experimental design and linear mixed-effects model. Our best  classification network achieved a mean accuracy of 83% (sensitivity 71%, specificity 91%) on external  datasets. TS plaques within the tympanic membrane often appear  as a semicircular crescent white plaque within the tym- panic membrane [2]. The prevalence of tympanosclerosis  in chronic otitis media (COM) has been reported from 9 to  38%. Relative to the quantity of calcification and its distur- bance of the ossicular chain movement, the patients experi- ence different degrees of conductive hearing loss. The etiol- ogy of TS has not been revealed completely [3]. However,  infection, physical trauma, myringotomy incisions, applica- tion of ventilation tube, chemical agents, metabolic changes,  genetic factors, and immunological reactions are considered  as responsible factors for this disease [4].

Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease  characterized by accumulation of lipids together with pen- etration of immunocytes, inflammatory cells, and calcium  deposits in the walls of medium and large-sized arteries,  wherein the arterial walls become thicker and lose their elas- ticity [5]. Endothelial cells, intimate smooth muscle cells,  and leukocytes have key roles in the progress of AS [6].  AS is a slow advancing and progressive disease, starting  from childhood. Various factors have been suggested as the  cause of this disease including hyperlipidemia, hypertension,  smoking, infection with bacteria and viruses, diabetes mel- litus, obesity, and genetic and habitual factors [7, 8].

Although TS and AS appears in two different organs,  they share similar histopathological and physiopathological  elements, and historically, many experts have known these  two processes as identical [9]. In both diseases, it is not  precisely recognized what starts the lesion principally [10].  Interestingly, some previous studies revealed relationship  between these diseases, and showed that AS patients had sta- tistically significant rate of TS in comparison to the normal  population. Pirodda et al. showed around 22.5% of hyper- cholesterolemia patients (4.9% in control subjects) and 36%  of patients underwent carotid endarterectomy (12% in con- trol group) had TS on otoscopy [10, 11]. In another study,  homocysteine, low-density lipoprotein, total cholesterol, and  triglyceride levels in 61 COM patients with TS plaques were  higher compared with those without TS plaques (p < 0.05)  and right and left internal carotid artery intima-media thick- ness was greater significantly (p = 0.001). In conclusion,  AS and TS were associated with identical risk factors [12].  These studies emphasized that there must be similar risk  factors triggering pathogenesis in both diseases [13].

TS is a progressive disorder, which appears to be the  main response of the tympanic membrane pars tensa to pro- longed sterile otitis media with effusion [14], and most of  the patients suffering from TS have earlier exposure to recur- rent serous otitis media (SOM), acute otitis media (AOM),  or chronic otitis media (COM) [15]. According to previous  studies, nitric oxide, free oxygen radicals, and catalase may  have a role in the development of TS in COM [16, 17]. Some  other studies revealed that the alteration in expressions of

transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1) and matrix metal- loproteinase-9 (MMP-9) involved in the formation of TS,  which may represent an important mechanism underlying  the pathogenesis of TS [18, 19]. Another study declared that  an association between C. pneumoniae or H. pylori infection  and the development of TS or other types of COM could not  be established [3]. Also, it has been generally believed that  bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Mycoplasma  pneumoniae involve in AOM and COM as well as in occur- rence of inflammatory process such as AS. Mycoplasma  pneumonia causes common respiratory tract infections, and  up to one-third of patients with Mycoplasma pneumonia  infection may have ear infection, although without positive  middle-ear fluid PCR [19]. This may partly be caused by dif- ficulties in culturing this fastidious organism. Nevertheless,  otitis media is often mentioned as a clinical condition asso- ciated with serologically verified M. pneumoniae infection.  Many studies in the past have shown the presence of Myco- plasma in cardiovascular diseases and middle-ear infections  in children and adults [20, 21].
The toxins such as ExoS and ExoU which are secreted  by type 3 secretion system (T3SS) of bacteria are the key  component responsible for TS, AOM, and COM [22, 23].

Due to development of calcification in both diseases,  evaluation of bone remodeling markers is a priority for  understanding the pathogenesis of these diseases. Different  factors influence differentiation and activation of osteoblasts,  and one of the most important ones is bone morphogenetic  proteins (BMPs). BMPs are the largest family of the TGF-β  superfamily and originally were recognized for their abil- ity in induction of bone formation, but it has known they  expressed in many tissues and have a role in a wide range  of processes including cellular proliferation and differen- tiation, adipogenesis, skeletal development, formation and  maintenance of vascular systems, and cancers [24]. A few  studies were done on the role of some well-known BMPs,  such as BMP-2, BMP-4, BMP-5, and BMP-7 in AS or TS,  but there are not any data about BMP-8a in these diseases  [25–27]. BMP-8a is induced in osteoblast differentiation and  osteogenesis phase of bone repair, and is highly expressed  in osteosarcoma [28, 29].

The plaques of TS and AS are reported to have calcium  phosphate structure [30]. Scanning electron microscopy  (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS)  can reveal the chemical structures and surface morphology  of these plaques. Koç and Üneri compared ultrastructures  of tympanosclerosis and atherosclerosis by light and elec- tron microscopy. They concluded that both specimen groups  were similar in terms of calcified area, collagen fibers, and  fibroblast [31].
As there were several similarities between the TS and AS  plaques, and also, due to controversies existed in revealing  other infective factors in pathogenesis of TS plaques [3],

On the other hand, 18  AS samples were taken from 18 patients suffered from AS  disease of the carotid artery that admitted for carotid endar- terectomy (14 males, 4 females, aged 48–72 years). None of  the COM cases had cholesteatoma and active otorrhea, no  one had history of previous ear surgery, and none of the TS  and AS patients received any topical or systemic antibiotics  at least 1 month before the surgery. All the patients signed  the informed consent before entering the study. After sur- gery, each sample was split into three parts for chemical,  microbial, and Immunohistochemical analyses, respectively.  To be cost-effective, only seven samples of each group were  randomly selected for SEM and EDXS analysis.
Chemical analysis

Seven samples of each group were selected for chemical  analysis. The samples were incubated in normal saline solu- tion. Topology of each plaque was assessed using SEM and  elemental analysis was done by EDXS. Chemical contents  of the plaques were compared, statistically.

1. Introduction

Otitis media (OM) represents a heterogeneous group of infectious and inflammatory diseases affecting the middle ear and remains one of the most common conditions encoun- tered in otolaryngology practice [1]. Clinically, OM is broadly classified into acute otitis media (AOM) and chronic otitis media (COM), each with distinct pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management strategies. AOM is an acute inflammatory condition, most frequently caused by bacterial pathogens. The diagnosis of AOM relies on a combination of clinical symptoms—such as acute ear pain, fever, and irritability—and otoscopic findings demonstrating middle ear effusion with signs of acute inflammation [2]. Management primarily focuses on pain control and appropriate antibiotic therapy. In contrast, COM is characterized by persistent or recurrent inflammation of the middle ear, often associated with chronic otorrhea through a perforated tympanic membrane. Diagnosis is usually es- tablished through otoscopic identification of tympanic membrane perforation and ongoing purulent discharge. Treatment strategies for COM commonly involve topical antibiotic ther- apy to control infection and achieve a dry ear, followed by surgical repair. Tympanoplasty is frequently performed to restore tympanic membrane integrity, with reported closure rates of approximately 83–87% [3]. In cases complicated by cholesteatoma, surgical removal is mandatory, as it remains the only definitive treatment and is essential for preventing progressive bone erosion and intracranial complications [4].

Although otoscopy is the cornerstone of OM diagnosis, its interpretation is inher- ently subjective and highly dependent on clinician experience and training. Variability in diagnostic accuracy, limited access to specialist expertise, and the increasing concern of antibiotic overuse and resistance highlight the need for more objective, standardized, and reproducible diagnostic tools [5]. In recent years, deep neural networks and other machine learning (ML) approaches have demonstrated considerable potential in the automated analysis of medical images, including the detection of tympanic membrane abnormalities from otoscopic images [6,7]. Among these approaches, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown particular effectiveness due to their ability to learn complex spatial and textural features directly from visual data. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven semantic segmentation into otologic imaging analysis offers a promising av- enue for improving diagnostic accuracy, consistency, and efficiency in clinical practice [8]. However, most previously published studies have relied on manually preselected otoscopic images that explicitly contain the tympanic membrane. This human-dependent region- of-interest (ROI) selection process inevitably introduces selection bias and limits both the reproducibility of AI training and the generalizability of the resulting models. In real-world clinical practice, otoscopic images frequently do not adequately visualize the tympanic membrane or are contaminated by cerumen or suboptimal imaging angles, which poses a significant challenge for practical AI deployment. In contrast, the proposed framework is capable of automatically determining whether a valid tympanic membrane is present within an input image. This design feature enhances robustness in real-world clinical settings and represents a critical step toward the practical implementation of AI-assisted otoscopic diagnostics.

The primary objective of this study is threefold. First, we aim to evaluate and compare the performance of four state-of-the-art semantic segmentation architectures—PSPNet, HRNet, DeepLabV3+ with a ResNet backbone, and U-Net—in the automatic detection and precise segmentation of tympanic membrane structures from clinical otoscopic images. The accuracy of these models will be assessed by their ability to correctly identify regions of interest (ROIs) relative to non-ROI areas, thereby determining the most reliable architecture for tympanic membrane segmentation. Second, following automated segmentation, we will perform feature extraction using deep learning-based and conventional ML techniques applied to the segmented anatomical regions. By analyzing color, texture, and structural features within predefined tympanic membrane subregions, the proposed framework aims to distinguish between normal ears, AOM, and COM with tympanic membrane perforation requiring surgical intervention. This region-based analytical strategy is designed to more closely reflect clinical reasoning and to enhance diagnostic interpretability. Finally, in light of the heightened risks associated with in-person clinical evaluations during the COVID-19 pandemic and potential future outbreaks of respiratory infectious diseases, this study seeks to address the growing demand for non-invasive, remote, and automated diagnostic tools. By leveraging AI-assisted analysis of otoscopic images, the proposed system has the potential to support clinical decision-making, facilitate early and accurate diagnosis, reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, and ultimately improve patient outcomes and promote health in both routine and resource-limited healthcare settings.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Data Procurement and Semi-Supervised Learning

This study performed AI-based image analysis using a dataset composed exclusively of clinical otoscopic images. From January 2020 to December 2021, otoscopic images were retrospectively collected from 607 patients aged 20–80 years. The dataset comprised 220 normal otoscopic images, 157 images of AOM, and 230 images of COM with tym- panic membrane perforation requiring surgical intervention. Among the total dataset, 485 images (79.9%) were manually annotated and used for model training. Semantic seg- mentation was performed on five anatomically relevant regions: the external auditory canal, tympanic ring, pars tensa, pars flaccida, and handle of the malleus. All regions were carefully delineated and labeled by a board-certified otolaryngologist. To ensure annotation accuracy and consistency, each segmentation mask underwent independent verification by three additional otolaryngologists, thereby establishing a standardized and reliable ground truth. The remaining 122 images (20.1%) were withheld for validation and testing, enabling objective performance evaluation on unseen data. In addition to images containing clearly visible tympanic membranes, a subset of images intentionally lacking an identifiable tympanic membrane was also collected from the aforementioned 220 normal cases. These images were designated as “invalid otoscopic images” and were deliberately included in the dataset to train the model to distinguish between diagnostically valid and invalid images, thereby improving its robustness and real-world applicability in clinical settings. To further evaluate model generalizability, external validation was performed using an independent dataset collected from another hospital, comprising 52 cases acquired with a different endoscopic imaging system. To maximize the utility of both labeled and unlabeled data, a semi-supervised learning strategy incorporating pseudo-labeling was adopted. Initially, a CNN was trained using the manually labeled images to establish a baseline model. This model was then applied to unlabeled images, where class probabilities were estimated by minimizing entropy to reduce uncertainty and class overlap. 2.2. Color and Texture Feature Extraction

Following semantic segmentation, chromatic and texture features were extracted from the 485 annotated otoscopic images, including 176 normal cases, 125 AOM cases, and 184 COM cases. Feature extraction was performed independently for each of the five segmented anatomical regions. Color analysis focused on six chromatic parameters: Red (R), Green (G), Blue (B), Hue (H), Chroma Blue (Cb), and Chroma Red (Cr). These parameters were selected to capture disease-related color variations across the tympanic membrane and surrounding structures. Statistical analyses were conducted on each region to characterize condition-specific chromatic patterns. Texture features were extracted using the Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), which quantifies spatial relationships between pixel gray levels and is well suited for assessing structural changes associated with inflammation. The complete system pipeline begins with semantic segmentation of otoscopic images to identify the five regions of interest within the tympanic membrane. As part of the proposed framework, the system was intentionally designed to first determine whether an input image constituted a clinically meaningful otoscopic image, defined by the presence of recognizable ear anatomy.
